paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) made in Yunnan in 1980. The record does not name the mountain or the factory. The year places it in the decades after 1949, when pu’er was made in [state factories](sheng:history) to standard recipes and sold under the state tea company’s labels.

Raw pu’er is never put through shou’s quick fermentation. It [changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging), so the forty-six years since it was pressed are part of this cake’s history. The trade has no agreed point where [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing) begins: some count from ten years, many from twenty. This cake is well past both. Heat and humidity set how fast that change runs, which is why [where a cake is kept](sheng:storage) shapes it as much as its age does.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
